---
title: "Crossfades"
description: "Fade one clip's sound into the next across a transition, choose the shape of the fade, and crossfade clips that have no picture."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

When two clips on a track overlap with a transition, the transition can fade the outgoing sound out and the incoming sound in, so the cut isn't heard as a jump.

<AtAGlance
  where="Clip tab ▸ Clip sub-tab ▸ Transition section"
  tools="set_transition_style"
/>

## Crossfade audio

A transition Frame Job makes already crossfades its sound, at the **+3 dB** shape, so most of the time there's nothing to do. Open the section to turn the crossfade off, or to change its shape.

<Steps>

1. Select the later of the two overlapping clips, on its own. The **Transition** section only appears for a single clip that overlaps the clip before it.

2. In the Clip tab, choose the **Clip** sub-tab and open **Transition**.

3. Tick or untick **Crossfade Audio**.

</Steps>

| **Crossfade Audio** | What you hear across the overlap |
| --- | --- |
| On | The outgoing sound fades out and the incoming sound fades in. If only one of the two clips has sound, that clip still fades. |
| Off | Both clips play at their own level for the whole overlap, mixed together. |

The fade follows the transition's **Curve**, so an eased transition eases its sound too. A transition Frame Job makes is **Ease In Out**. **Curve** and **Crossfade Audio** are separate settings, and changing one leaves the other alone.

Changing the overlap's length is the **Duration** row. See [The Transition section](/motion/transition-settings/).

## Choose a crossfade shape

**Crossfade Shape** sets the curve of the fade. It's available while **Crossfade Audio** is on, and the default is **+3 dB**. The incoming clip follows the shape, and the outgoing clip follows it in reverse.

| **Crossfade Shape** | Use it for | Each clip's level halfway through the fade |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **+3 dB** | Two unrelated takes. It holds the level steady across the overlap. | About −3 dB |
| **Linear** | Two parts of the same sound. A straight-line pair, which dips 3 dB in the middle of unrelated takes. | About −6 dB |
| **S-Curve** | A fade that does most of its changing in the middle of the overlap and moves slowly at both ends. | About −6 dB |
| **−3 dB** | A slow start. The incoming sound rises late and the outgoing sound falls early, so the middle of the overlap is the quietest of the four. | About −11 dB |

## Audio-only transitions

Two overlapping clips with no picture get the same **Transition** section, on the same sub-tab. Only their sound changes. **Crossfade Audio**, **Crossfade Shape** and **Curve** control the fade, **Duration** sets its length, and **Kind** has no visible effect.

An edit that makes one clip overlap the one before it adds a transition for audio clips as it does for any other, so overlapping two music clips crossfades them straight away. See [Add or remove a transition](/motion/add-a-transition/) for the other ways to make one.

## Crossfade after Detach Audio

[Detach Audio](/audio/detach-and-attach/) switches the sound off on the picture clip, so **Crossfade Audio** on a transition between two picture clips does nothing after that. To crossfade the sound, overlap the detached audio clips and give them a transition of their own.

## Good to know

- The crossfade multiplies whatever else is happening to the sound. Mute, solo, ducking, volume and a clip's own fades still apply on top.
- With **Kind** set to **None**, an overlap has no stored transition. It draws as a linear cross dissolve with no sound crossfade, and the section shows **Linear** and **Crossfade Audio** off. Changing either of them stores a transition with exactly the values shown.
- Choosing another style from **Clip ▸ Transition** on a clip that already overlaps keeps its curve and its crossfade.
- A transition on a nest clip fades all the sound inside the nest. A crossfade between clips inside the nest still happens too, and you hear both.
- Each clip's [limiter](/audio/limiter/) holds that clip alone, so two limited clips can add up past the ceiling during an overlap. An export's master limiter catches this, but the preview has none, so it can sound louder while you edit. A [track compressor or limiter](/audio/track-dynamics/) is also approximate in the preview where clips overlap.

## Related

- [The Transition section](/motion/transition-settings/)
- [Audio fades](/audio/fades/)
- [Detach and Attach Audio](/audio/detach-and-attach/)
- [J-cuts and L-cuts](/audio/j-and-l-cuts/)

---
title: "Pan and Mix to mono"
description: "Move a stereo clip's balance left or right, fold its channels into one, and place a sound anywhere between the speakers."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

The **Mix** section places a clip's sound between the speakers. **Pan** moves a stereo clip's balance, and **Mix to mono** folds its channels into one.

<AtAGlance
  where="Clip tab ▸ Sound sub-tab ▸ Mix section"
  tools="set_audio"
/>

The section's header summarises it: "centre", "mono", or the pan position. **Detach Audio** and **Attach Audio** are on the same section, and have [their own page](/audio/detach-and-attach/).

## Pan a clip

Drag **Pan**, type a number from −100 to 100, or use a quick pick: −100, −50, 0, 50 or 100. Negative numbers go left, positive numbers go right, and the default is 0.

**Position**, under it, reads the result in words: "centre", "left 30" or "right 100". It's a read-out, so there's nothing to set there.

On a stereo clip, **Pan** is a balance control. It doesn't move the left channel's sound across to the right:

- At the centre, nothing changes.
- Moving it one way turns that side up and the other side down, keeping the total power steady.
- At −100 or 100, the side it went to is about 3 dB louder than at the centre, and the other side is silent.

Pan has no effect on a mono file. See [Good to know](#good-to-know).

## Mix to mono

**Mix to mono** averages all of the clip's channels into one and sends that to every channel. It's off by default.

On a one-channel file it does nothing, because there's nothing to fold.

If only one channel of a stereo file has anything on it, use [Channels](/audio/channels/) instead. Averaging a voice with a silent channel halves its level.

## Place a stereo clip's sound anywhere

To hear a true pan, tick **Mix to mono** as well as setting **Pan**. The fold happens before the pan, so both channels carry the same sound, and **Pan** places that one sound anywhere from left to right.

## Animate them

With an [action](/motion/edit-an-action/) selected, both controls write what the action changes to. **Pan** glides there across the action. **Mix to mono** is a switch, so it changes at the action's end, and its row says "at end". See [Animate sound with actions](/audio/animate-sound/).

## Reset the section

**Reset** on the section's header sets the pan back to centre and turns mono off. It appears while the section differs from its default. See [Reset a section](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#reset-a-section).

## Good to know

- Pan has no effect on a mono file, with or without **Mix to mono**. Such a clip only becomes stereo after the point where Pan acts. A [track's pan](/audio/track-volume-and-pan/) can't move it either.
- On a nest clip, **Pan** has no effect. Set it on the clips inside.
- **Mix to mono** on a nest clip does work: it folds everything inside the nest, and that flattens any panning on the clips and tracks in it.
- The Volume section's **Loudness** read-out counts Pan and Mix to mono on a stereo clip, and so does [Normalize](/audio/normalize/) in Loudness mode.
- In the clip's chain of sound processing, this section comes after the [compressor](/audio/compressor/) and before the [limiter](/audio/limiter/).

## Related

---
title: "Channels"
description: "Choose which channels of a stereo file play, to fix a microphone recorded on one side or swap left and right."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

**Channels** chooses which channels of a stereo file a clip plays. It's the fix for a microphone recorded onto one side of a stereo file, which otherwise plays from one speaker only.

<AtAGlance
  where="Clip tab ▸ Sound sub-tab ▸ Channels section"
  tools="set_audio"
/>

## Choose channels

Open the **Channels** section and pick from **Play**. With several clips selected, the choice goes to all of them.

| **Play** | What you hear |
| --- | --- |
| **Both** | The file as it is. This is the default. |
| **Left Only** | The left channel, from both speakers. |
| **Right Only** | The right channel, from both speakers. |
| **Swap Left and Right** | The two channels exchanged. |

For a microphone on one channel, choose **Left Only** or **Right Only**. The voice then plays from both speakers at its own level. [Mix to mono](/audio/pan-and-mono/#mix-to-mono) would also put it in both speakers, but averaging it with the silent channel halves its level.

The header of the section shows the current choice. **Reset** there puts it back to **Both**.

## Good to know

- A mono file has only one channel, so the choice has no effect on it.
- On a nest clip the choice has no effect. Set it on the clips inside.
- The Volume section's **Loudness** read-out counts the choice, and so does [Normalize](/audio/normalize/) in Loudness mode. Normalize in Peak mode reads the file's waveform and doesn't.
- The choice comes right after [voice isolation](/audio/voice-isolation/), and before the [EQ](/audio/eq/) and [Mix to mono](/audio/pan-and-mono/#mix-to-mono).
- On a stereo file, a reverb or echo [voice effect](/audio/voice-effects/) mixes the two channels, so the choice picks from the effected pair.
- With an [action](/motion/edit-an-action/) selected, the choice is what the action changes to. It switches at the action's end with no glide, and its row says "at end".

## Related

- [Pan and Mix to mono](/audio/pan-and-mono/)
- [The Sound tab](/audio/sound-tab/)
- [Normalize](/audio/normalize/)

---
title: "Normalize"
description: "Set each selected clip's volume from a measurement of the clip, to a loudness target that matches clips or to a peak level."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Normalize sets each selected clip's volume from a measurement of the clip, so you don't have to set levels by ear. In its default Loudness mode, every clip lands at the same loudness, which is how you make clips match.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Normalize"
  where="Clip tab ▸ Sound sub-tab ▸ Volume section"
  tools="normalize_clip"
/>

<Shot
  name="09-clip-sound.inspector"
  alt="The Sound sub-tab's Volume section for an audio clip: Volume at 100%, a Gain of +0.0 dB, Loudness and At volume both reading −21.8 LUFS and −20.8 dBTP, a Mute checkbox, a Normalize row set to Loudness at −16.0 LUFS, and the Normalize and Enhance Voice buttons."
/>

## Normalize a clip

<Steps>

1. Select one or more clips.

2. On the **Sound** sub-tab, open the **Volume** section and check the **Normalize** row: the mode, and in Loudness mode the target.

3. Press **Normalize**, or choose **Clip ▸ Normalize**. The two do the same thing and follow that row.

</Steps>

However many clips are selected, it's one undo step, named "Normalize". That step also takes back any limiter it turned on.

It replaces the clip's volume rather than adding to it, so pressing it a second time changes nothing, and that second press beeps. **Mute** is left as it is.

## Choose a mode

The first control in the **Normalize** row picks what Normalize aims at.

| Mode | What it aims at | Matches clips? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Loudness** | Each clip's overall loudness reaches the target, −16 LUFS unless you choose another. This is the default. | Yes |
| **Peak** | Each clip's loudest moment reaches −1 dBFS. | No |

The mode and the target belong to the app, not the project. They're kept between launches, and changing them isn't an undo step.

## Set the loudness target

The field beside the mode sets the level in LUFS, from −50 to −5. The default is −16, and it's only live in Loudness mode. The quick picks are:

| Target | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| −14 LUFS | YouTube's playback reference |
| −16 LUFS | The default |
| −23 LUFS | The EBU R 128 broadcast level |

[Enhance Voice](/audio/enhance-voice/) aims at the same target, and the [Loudness Meter](/audio/loudness-meter/) draws it as a line.

## Loudness mode

Loudness mode sets each clip's volume so its integrated loudness, the BS.1770 measure of the clip as a whole as the export plays it, reaches the target. The volume can go down as well as up.

- **It watches the peaks.** A clip whose true peak would pass −1 dBTP at that volume gets its [Limiter](/audio/limiter/) turned on at −1 dBTP in the same step, and the volume is the one that reaches the target through the limiter.
- **It keeps a limiter you set.** A clip that already has one keeps it, with its ceiling lowered to −1 dBTP if it was higher.
- **It stops at 3200 %.** A clip that would need more stops there and lands quieter than the target.

## Peak mode

Peak mode sets each clip's volume so its loudest moment reaches −1 dBFS. The level is fixed, and it happens at once, with no sheet.

Each clip gets its own gain, so levels don't match across a selection: a sparse voice still sounds quieter than a dense one. A clip whose peak is quieter than about −31 dBFS can't reach −1 dBFS. It's turned up to 3200 % and stops there.

## What Normalize measures

Normalize measures the clip, not the mix. It reads the clip's waveform (Peak) or loudness analysis (Loudness) over the part of the file that actually plays, so a trimmed clip is measured on what's left.

The clip's volume, fades, ducking, mute and solo don't affect the reading, and neither do its track's volume and pan. In Loudness mode, the clip's own **Channels**, **Mix to mono** and **Pan** do count on a stereo clip. A mono clip is measured on both channels, as the export plays it, which reads 3 dB louder than the file on its own.

## Measure through a clip's processing

Cleaning up a clip changes how loud it measures, so the analysis alone would miss the target. In Loudness mode, a clip with any of these is rendered through them as the export plays it, and its volume is set from what comes out:

- An active [EQ](/audio/eq/)
- [Hum removal](/audio/hum-removal/)
- [Voice isolation](/audio/voice-isolation/)
- [Noise reduction](/audio/noise-reduction/)
- A [gate](/audio/gate/)
- The [leveller](/audio/leveller/)
- A [de-esser](/audio/de-esser/)
- A [compressor](/audio/compressor/)
- A [voice effect](/audio/voice-effects/)

With the limiter on as well, Normalize renders again at the volume it chose, and adjusts until the result is within 0.1 LU of the target, at most three times. A clip that already has that limiter keeps its volume when the new one is within 0.05 dB, so a second press still changes nothing.

This takes a moment per clip, longer on a long clip, and the first press waits for the clip's voice isolation or voice effect to render. A clip with none of this processing is measured from the analysis at once.

Until Normalize or Enhance Voice has measured such a clip, the **At volume** read-out shows "≈" in front of its figures, because they're from before the processing. See [Clip volume](/audio/volume/).

## The Measuring Sound sheet

While clips are rendered through their processing, a **Measuring Sound** sheet shows a progress bar and "Clip 1 of 2…", counting only the clips that need a render. Editing commands are off until it closes. [Enhance Voice](/audio/enhance-voice/) and [Match Audio](/audio/match-audio/) use the same sheet.

Nothing changes until every clip is measured, and **Cancel** leaves everything as it is. If the project changes while it measures, nothing changes, Frame Job beeps, and a sentence at the foot of the inspector says to choose the command again.

## Clips Normalize skips

Normalize leaves out the clips below and still does the rest. The button and the menu item are dimmed when no selected clip plays sound, or when only nests are selected. A press that changes nothing beeps, and neither the button nor the menu says which clips were skipped or why.

| Skipped | Why | Mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nests | Their level lives in the clips inside them. Open the nest and normalize those, or set the nest clip's volume by hand. | Both |
| Shapes, titles, stills and movies with no sound | There's no sound to measure. A clip with its sound switched off counts too. | Both |
| A clip not analysed yet | Its waveform or loudness is still being worked out, which often happens straight after an import. The **Loudness** read-out says "measuring…" meanwhile. | Both |
| A silent clip | It's silent over the part that plays. In Loudness mode that means quieter than −70 LUFS throughout. | Both |
| A very short clip | It plays for under 0.4 s, too short for a loudness measurement. | Loudness |
| A clip whose reversed copy is still being made | It can't be rendered yet. | Loudness, through processing |
| A clip whose processing can't be rendered | There's nothing to measure. | Loudness, through processing |
| A clip that's too quiet after its processing | It's quieter than −70 LUFS after it. | Loudness, through processing |

## Good to know

- Normalize writes the clip's base level, even with the playhead inside an action. With an action selected, the button carries a small boxed "clip" tag to show this. If an action animates the volume, its values still win for as long as it runs.
- It can go past the slider's 400 %, up to the 3200 % ceiling, about +30 dB.
- The result for a limited clip with no other processing is worked out from the analysis, not rendered. The export lands within a few tenths of a LU of it.
- A clip played at a speed other than ×1, or ramped, reads to within about 0.5 LU of what plays. A file with more than two channels is measured from a two-channel mix of it.

## With an agent

`normalize_clip` names its own mode and doesn't read the **Normalize** row. In Peak mode it can aim anywhere from −60 to 0 dBFS, and it answers what each clip measured, where it landed, and each skipped clip with its reason. See [Tools: audio](/mcp/tools-audio/).

## Related

- [Enhance Voice](/audio/enhance-voice/)
- [Match Audio](/audio/match-audio/)
- [Clip volume](/audio/volume/)
- [Limiter](/audio/limiter/)
- [Export loudness](/export/loudness/)

---
title: "Enhance Voice"
description: "Measure a voice recording and set up its cleaning, dynamics and volume in one step, with ordinary settings you can see and change."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Enhance Voice sets a clip up for speech in one step. It measures the voice and the pauses, chooses the clean-up and dynamics the recording needs, and sets the volume that reaches your loudness target.

<AtAGlance
  menu="Clip ▸ Enhance Voice"
  where="Clip tab ▸ Sound sub-tab ▸ Volume section"
  tools="enhance_voice"
  needs="Nothing. Speech detection and voice isolation run on your Mac, with no key and no upload."
/>

## Enhance a voice

<Steps>

1. Select one or more clips with speech in them.

2. Check the target in the **Normalize** row of the **Volume** section. It's −16 LUFS unless you've [chosen another](/audio/normalize/#set-the-loudness-target).

3. Press **Enhance Voice**, or choose **Clip ▸ Enhance Voice**.

4. Wait for the [Measuring Sound sheet](/audio/normalize/#the-measuring-sound-sheet) to finish.

</Steps>

However many clips are selected, it's one undo step, named "Enhance Voice". **Cancel** in the sheet changes nothing.

Everything it writes is an ordinary setting, so you can see and change each one in its own section. Pressing it again changes nothing and beeps, and so does [Normalize](/audio/normalize/) at the same target afterwards.

To run it on a recording as soon as the recording lands, see [Polish when a recording lands](/recording/when-it-lands/).

## What it measures

It reads the clip as recorded, before any of the settings it's about to write: its loudness and true peak, and, every 10 ms of the part that plays, whether the clip is speaking or pausing. It needs at least a second of speech, and half a second of pause to measure the noise between words.

## What it sets

These come in the order the sound passes through them, and each one is a separate decision.

### Rumble cut

Always. It sets the [EQ](/audio/eq/)'s **Rumble Cut**, a high-pass at 80 Hz, 24 dB/oct, and keeps the EQ's other parts.

### Noisy pauses

The pauses count as noisy when their median loudness is less than 45 dB under the voice.

| The pauses are | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Noisy | Turns on [voice isolation](/audio/voice-isolation/) at 80 % with noise reduction off, and fits a [gate](/audio/gate/) to the pauses. |
| Noisy, on a clip with a speed change, a ramp or a freeze frame | Turns on [noise reduction](/audio/noise-reduction/) at 50 % with voice isolation off, because isolation can't serve that clip, and fits the gate. |
| Quiet | Turns voice isolation, noise reduction and the gate off. |
| Under half a second long in total | Leaves all three as they are, because there's nothing to measure. |

The gate opens 10 dB above the pauses' median true peak, held between −40 and −6 dB from the clip's loudness.

### Leveller

It turns on the [leveller](/audio/leveller/) at its defaults when the speech's loudness varies a lot from moment to moment, meaning its short-term loudness range is over 6 LU. The range is measured over 3-second stretches of the speech alone. At or under 6 LU the leveller is turned off, and with under 3 seconds of speech it's left as it is.

### De-esser

It turns on the [de-esser](/audio/de-esser/) at its defaults when at least 5 % of the speech has a hot "s" band: 6 kHz and up, within 10 dB of the clip's loudness. Otherwise it's turned off.

### Compressor, limiter and final volume

- A [compressor](/audio/compressor/) at 3:1, its threshold at the speech's median true peak, with makeup that gives back the loudness it takes.
- The [limiter](/audio/limiter/). The clip keeps its own, with the ceiling at most −1 dBTP, or gets the default.
- The volume that takes the clip to the **Normalize** row's target, measured through everything above as the export plays it. It's checked by rendering, to within 0.1 LU, up to three times.

The target is used even when the row is set to Peak and the field is dimmed. Enhance Voice always aims at a loudness.

## What it leaves alone

Hum removal, the channel choice, pan, mono, fades, ducking, **Mute**, **Keep pitch** and the EQ's other parts all stay as they are. Like Normalize, it writes the clip's base settings, even with the playhead inside an action.

## Clips Enhance Voice skips

It's offered where [Normalize](/audio/normalize/#clips-normalize-skips) is, and it leaves out the same clips as Normalize in Loudness mode, plus two more. The rest of the selection is still enhanced. With nothing to enhance, the press beeps, and neither the button nor the menu says why.

| Skipped | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A clip that plays no sound, or a nest | There's no voice of its own to measure. Open a nest to enhance the clips inside. |
| A clip that plays for under 0.4 s | It's too short for a loudness measurement. |
| A clip quieter than −70 LUFS, before or after its processing | There's no voice to work with. |
| A clip with under 1 second of speech | There's too little to measure a voice from. |
| A clip not analysed yet | See [Wait for analysis](#wait-for-analysis). |
| A clip whose reversed copy is still being made | It can't be rendered yet. |
| A clip whose processing can't be rendered | There's nothing to measure. |

## Wait for analysis

Enhance Voice needs two results that are worked out on your Mac after a file is imported: the clip's loudness and its speech. A clip without both yet is skipped, which often happens straight after an import. The **Loudness** read-out says "measuring…" while the loudness is still running. Wait a moment and press again.

## Check its gate by ear

Enhance Voice sets the gate from the pauses it measured. On a voice with very soft word starts, the gate can bite into them, so listen to those words and lower the [gate](/audio/gate/)'s threshold if you need to.

## Good to know

- Applying the rumble cut also takes the EQ out of bypass if you'd bypassed it.
- Every selected clip gets its limiter on, because the volume is solved through it.
- Measuring takes time in proportion to the clip's length, and it waits for the clip's voice isolation to render first.
- The settings come from the clip's own measurements, so two clips in a selection can end up with different settings.

## With an agent

`enhance_voice` takes its own target rather than the **Normalize** row's. It answers what it measured for each clip, exactly which settings it wrote, and one sentence per rule saying why, so an agent can tell you what the button doesn't. Each skipped clip comes back with its reason. See [Tools: audio](/mcp/tools-audio/).

## Related

- [Normalize](/audio/normalize/)
- [Match Audio](/audio/match-audio/)
- [Voice Isolation](/audio/voice-isolation/)
- [The Sound tab](/audio/sound-tab/)
- [Polish when a recording lands](/recording/when-it-lands/)
